Hey everyone! I’m Ahmed, a Computer Science undergrad specializing in backend architecture, data automation, and AI integrations.

I’m locked in on the Harmonization of MODIS & VIIRS Hot Spots challenge! If we team up, I guarantee a rock-solid backend for a killer live demo.

No specific tech stack required! If you’re insanely passionate, ready to hustle, and want to crush the frontend, data, or our final pitch, you belong here. Let’s build something epic! Beginners are more than welcome!
summary: Stack is a multi-sensor spatio-temporal fire regime analytics platform that resolves the historical "sensor-shift distortion" between NASA’s 1 km MODIS (2000–present) and 375 m VIIRS (2012–present) active fire datasets. details:
What it does and how it works: Stack is an end-to-end data pipeline and interactive web dashboard designed to solve the "camera illusion" in NASA's historical fire tracking data. When NASA launched the VIIRS sensor in 2012, its 375m resolution was so much sharper than the older 1km MODIS sensor that it began counting multiple sub-pixels for a single fire. If you plot raw NASA data on a timeline, it looks like global fires artificially spiked by 300% overnight in 2012.

Our system solves this through a three-step harmonization algorithm:

  1. Filtering: We isolate true vegetation/crop fires using NASA's type=0 flag, stripping out stationary industrial gas flares and low-confidence thermal noise.
  2. Spatial Co-Aggregation: We mathematically force the high-resolution VIIRS pixels onto a unified 0.01° x 0.01° (approx. 1km) daily spatial grid, collapsing multiple VIIRS sub-pixels over the same fire into a single "Fire Cell-Day."
  3. Monthly Calibration ($\alpha_m$): By analyzing the 2012–2018 period when both satellites flew simultaneously, our pipeline calculates an empirical monthly scaling ratio. We use this to scale VIIRS sensitivity down so it perfectly matches the 25-year historical MODIS baseline.

Benefits and Intended Impact: Before Stack, disaster managers and environmental departments comparing recent fire activity to the early 2000s were essentially comparing two different rulers. By mathematically removing the 2012 sensor jump, our project provides one continuous, unbiased 25-year record.

For Pakistan specifically, this allows local governments and researchers to accurately track the severity of the October–November rice-stubble burning season in Punjab (which drives regional smog) and the agricultural fires in the Indus Delta, answering definitively whether the current season is worse than the 25-year historical median.

Tools and Tech Stack: We processed over 1.28 million real NASA FIRMS fire records for Pakistan (2000–2026). Our technology stack includes:

  • Data Engineering: Python, Pandas, and NumPy for spatial gridding, filtering, and statistical calibration.
  • Backend API: FastAPI to serve the harmonized datasets instantly.
  • Frontend Dashboard: HTML, JavaScript, Tailwind CSS for styling, and Leaflet.js with keyless Esri base maps for spatial bounding and interactive geospatial visualization.

How our project is creative: Instead of just plotting the raw data onto a map, we took a rigorous data-engineering approach to solve the root problem of sensor discrepancy. Our creativity lies in our "Blind Holdout Test." To prove our calibration wasn't just overfitting the data, we trained our algorithm purely on the 2012–2018 overlap period, and then tested it "blind" on 2019–2025 data. Our predicted harmonized counts matched the actual MODIS ground truth almost 1:1.

We also designed the UX/UI to be accessible and intuitive for non-technical policymakers, utilizing a colorblind-safe (Viridis) 25-year heatmap calendar, real-time median anomaly calculations, and an interactive "draw-a-box" map filter that works entirely in the browser.

Factors our team considered: We heavily considered performance, accessibility, and local context. Processing over 1.2 million rows live in a browser would cause lag, so we decoupled our architecture: Python pre-aggregates the spatial cubes offline, ensuring our web dashboard loads in milliseconds. We also considered the diurnal cycle—since Terra passes in the morning and Aqua/VIIRS pass in the afternoon, our 24-hour UTC calendar-day grouping naturally eliminates double-counting across different overpass times.
